Nociceptor

Noradrenaline released by descending fibres from the brainstem acts on α2A adrenoceptors on the central terminals of nociceptors. Through Gi, the receptor inhibits adenylate cyclase and closes calcium channels, so less glutamate and substance P is released onto dorsal horn neurons. Drugs that raise spinal noradrenaline, such as duloxetine, reduce knee OA pain.

Spinal nociceptive neuron

Descending noradrenaline also acts directly on dorsal horn neurons through α2 adrenoceptors, which couple to Gi and hyperpolarise the cell. Together with the presynaptic action on nociceptor terminals, this is the spinal pain inhibition that serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors strengthen. Duloxetine reduces knee OA pain, mainly in patients with signs of central sensitisation.

Colour

Proteins and metabolites are coloured by their contribution to pain: red for those that raise it (they excite or sensitise nociceptive neurons, or drive the inflammation that does), blue for those that relieve it, and olive for the shared signalling machinery (G proteins, RGS, adenylate cyclase, phospholipases, kinases, adaptors, second messengers, ions and nucleotides), whose effect is set by the receptor upstream. Drugs are yellow and classes of molecules white. Each molecule is coloured by its role in this block, so the same molecule can be red in one block and blue in another.

Here noradrenaline and the α2A receptor are blue: in the spinal cord noradrenaline from descending pathways suppresses pain through α2A receptors, while in injured tissue it has variable effects, including aggravation of pain (Pertovaara 2006). Noradrenaline is red in the β2 blocks.
